title: Orchid Finance - Dedicated Capacity Discovery
summary: Discovery focused on Redwood Dedicated: reserved GPUs, isolation needs, burst strategy, and scaling. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private; leaning dedicated for performance and data isolation. Security and compliance questions (KMS, SSO, audit logs) and a request for benchmark plan and pricing for a 3-month pilot.
topics: reserved GPU sizing and burst options
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 14:30 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood), Diego (Redwood), Tom (Orchid), Priya (Orchid), Aisha (Orchid), Ben (Orchid)

00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is maya from redwood, i'm the AE on this account, with diego and lena from eng, and samir who will help with onboarding.
00:12 Tom: thanks, maya. really appreciate it. we wanted to dig into dedicated capacity — reserved GPUs — and how that plays with our isolation needs.
00:20 Maya: cool, high level first, can you walk us through current stack and where you're running inference today?
00:28 Priya: sure, we run a mix; most of our models are on prem right now for PII reasons, we have kubernetes clusters with some gpu nodes, and we also use a managed endpoint on cloud for bursty jobs. It's a bit fragmented.
00:40 Diego: got it. are there specific SLOs you aim for? latency p95 or throughput per second?
00:47 Priya: target p95 under 200ms for our chat assistant when under normal load, and during peak we need to sustain ~120 concurrent requests with avg token lengths ~60. costs matter — we can't overprovision all the time.
01:02 Aisha: and from security side we need full audit logs, KMS integration for keys, SAML SSO, and basically SOC2 type controls. anything that touches customer data must be isolated.
01:12 Maya: completely understood. so dedicated is often chosen for that isolation and predictability. quick Q — do you plan to keep everything on dedicated or do you want hybrid routing (hosted for baseline, dedicated for sensitive workloads)?
01:24 Tom: leaning hybrid, baseline hosted for non-sensitive internal dev users to save cost, but customer facing flows must be on reserved/dedicated.
01:33 Ben: also we need burst capacity for heavy marketing days — can we burst beyond reserved without spinning up new infra for hours?
01:41 Lena: good question, redwood has burst policies — you can reserve a baseline GPU pool and allow controlled burst to shared capacity with limits; we'll go over typical burst patterns.
01:52 Diego: technically we support baseline reserved capacity and a configurable burst policy that either purchases ephemeral capacity or routes to a hosted tier with data handling controls. there are tradeoffs on isolation and egress.
02:06 Mei: how's data handled if we burst to hosted? is customer data persisted or mixed?
02:12 Diego: by default we recommend encrypting and using a policy that masks or strips PII for burst routes; if you need strict isolation, you can set a hard limit to never burst to shared hosted.
02:23 Priya: ok. can you talk about GPU sizing and model footprint? we plan to serve a mix of Llama-derivative and a couple smaller fine-tuned models, avg context 1k tokens when doing retrieval-augmented generation.
02:36 Diego: for 1k context and avg 60 token responses, and ~120 concurrents, rough throughput depends on model architecture and quantization. ballpark, for a 13B quantized we might need 8-12 A100-like slots; for 70B you could be in the 20+ reserved gpus range.
02:55 Tom: hmm that's a big delta. we are trying to avoid 70B on prod if cost not justified. what's the workflow to test this?
03:04 Maya: typical path is pilot: we provision a small dedicated pool (e.g., 4 gpus), run your evals and a short benchmark while diego tunes batching, KV cache, quantization profile. then scale up if needed.
03:18 Ben: what's the autoscaling time? we can't accept 10 minute cold starts.
03:24 Diego: autoscale is policy-driven; reserved pools are warm so scale up between sizes is faster. cold spin from zero is slower — we recommend some reserved baseline to avoid long tails.
03:36 Aisha: security: can we host the control plane in our VPC or must management plane touch public endpoints?
03:43 Lena: for Redwood Private you get a customer-managed control plane in a VPC. for Dedicated (hosted managed) we do offer a private control plane option for enterprise — it's an add-on.
03:55 Aisha: and KMS? we need customer keys, HSM preferably.
04:01 Diego: we integrate with customer KMS and several HSM providers. keys can be customer-managed; we can document exact flows.
04:10 Tom: any compliance certs we should know about?
04:14 Maya: SOC 2 Type II is standard for our dedicated and hosted offerings; we also have ISO in progress. we'll share the security pack after the call.
04:24 Priya: ok good. what about model versions and rollouts — we need safe rollouts and A/B tests with automatic fallback if latency exceeds SLO.
04:33 Diego: our rollout engine supports canary and A/B, and fallback policies. you can pin versions to pools too.
04:39 Priya: how about caching — can we cache per-customer prefix KV?
04:44 Diego: yes, we support prefix caching and per-customer KV caches; eviction policies are configurable and they significantly reduce cost for repeated prompts.
04:52 Mei: any constraints on privacy when using caching?
04:55 Diego: if caching persists on shared storage we'd recommend encrypted scopes; with dedicated pools caches can be tenant-isolated.
05:04 Tom: for the pilot we want to measure latency p95, cost per 1k tokens, and error rate.
05:10 Maya: perfect, we'll put together a benchmark plan. diego — can you outline the benchmark steps?
05:16 Diego: yeah. 1) we ask for a representative prompt set, 2) we run steady-state throughput tests, 3) peak-burst tests and 4) failure/recovery scenarios. we'll capture traces and token-level cost.
05:29 Tom: timeline? we want pilot started in 2–3 weeks if possible.
05:33 Maya: we can target that — need security review and pricing approval.
05:38 Aisha: security review: please send SOC2, pen test summary, list of subprocesors, and our security questionnaire filled out.
05:45 Maya: will do.
05:47 Ben: pricing model — reserved commit monthly or annual?
05:51 Maya: both; we offer monthly reserved capacity and discounts for annual commitments. pricing depends on GPU type, number of slots, and retention windows for KV cache.
06:02 Priya: curious about quantization support — will models need re-compile or is it automatic?
06:08 Diego: some quantizations require model conversion; we provide toolchain support and some auto-quantize paths, but we may recommend a specific quantized variant for best perf.
06:18 Tom: any vendor lock-in? we want to be able to move models between our on-prem and redwood dedicated.
06:23 Diego: we support standard model formats; we aim to keep you portable. dedicated deployment configs can be exported.
06:30 Priya: do you support tenant-level RBAC and audit logs?
06:33 Lena: yes, RBAC is configurable; audit logs are available and can be pushed to customer S3 or SIEM.
06:40 Aisha: encryption at rest details?
06:43 Diego: AES-256 at rest, and keys via KMS; we can support customer-managed keys so we never have plaintext access.
06:51 Mei: will there be network egress costs if we burst to hosted?
06:55 Maya: depends on routing and region; we'll include egress estimates in the pricing doc.
07:01 Tom: what about maintenance windows and SLA?
07:04 Maya: dedicated can have SLA-backed uptime and we can negotiate maintenance windows for enterprise deals.
07:10 Priya: for scaling expectations: say we start with 4 gpus reserved and the model needs 12 under load — how do you typically handle scale up?
07:19 Diego: we'll run controlled scale-up: bump to 8 then 12 as needed; autoscaler can add capacity automatically but it's best to plan a short warm-up period. cache warming also helps throughput.
07:30 Ben: can we reserve heterogenous GPUs? some workloads need more memory than others.
07:34 Lena: yes, pools can be configured with mixed GPU types, and routing policies can send certain models to specific GPU classes.
07:42 Tom: showstoppers? what might cause us to not go dedicated?
07:46 Maya: cost and admin overhead are common. if you can't commit to baseline reserved units, the unit economics might favor hosted. but given your isolation needs, dedicated is likely the right path.
07:58 Priya: ok. who owns the infra ops? we want minimal ops on our side.
08:03 Maya: Redwood manages the infra for hosted Dedicated; for Private you manage more. We'll propose a managed service add-on if you want hands-off.
08:12 Aisha: can you explain data residency — some customer data must remain in EU.
08:16 Diego: we have region pinning and can ensure dedicated pools run in specific regions; for Private on-prem it's obviously local.
08:23 Tom: great. let's talk concrete next steps.
08:26 Maya: recap: 1) Maya to send pricing and security pack, 2) Diego to share benchmark plan and test infra requirements, 3) customer to share prompt set and 1-week sample traffic, 4) schedule technical deep dive next week with infra folks.
08:44 Priya: can you also include an estimate for a 3-month pilot with 8 gpus baseline and burst to 16?
08:52 Maya: yes, will include that.
08:54 Aisha: and please answer the security questionnaire in-line.
08:58 Maya: will do.
09:00 Tom: timeline — can we have pricing + security pack by Friday this week?
09:05 Maya: yes, we'll aim for Thursday EOD.
09:08 Ben: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
09:11 Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs.
09:15 (meeting ends)

Notes: occasional mis-transcriptions present (e.g., K V cache -> K V cache; Llama variants sometimes transcribed as 'layer'); some speaker labels collapsed.
